title: Design Skiplist
description:
# Design Skiplist

Design a `Skiplist` class that stores integers and supports `search`, `add`, and `erase`.

A skiplist keeps several sorted linked-list levels. Level `0` contains every value. Higher levels contain selected promoted nodes, so a search can move right across a high level and then drop down near the target. Expected `search`, `add`, and `erase` time is O(log n) for a probabilistic skiplist.

Implement the `Skiplist` class:

* `Skiplist()` Initializes an empty skiplist.
* `boolean search(int target)` Returns `true` if `target` currently exists, otherwise returns `false`.
* `void add(int num)` Inserts one occurrence of `num`. Duplicate values are allowed.
* `boolean erase(int num)` Removes one occurrence of `num` if present and returns `true`; otherwise, it leaves the structure unchanged and returns `false`.

Do not use Java's built-in ordered collections as the main data structure.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1

**Input:**
["Skiplist", "add", "add", "add", "search", "add", "search", "erase", "erase", "search"]
[[], [1], [2], [3], [0], [4], [1], [0], [1], [1]]

**Output:**
[null, null, null, null, false, null, true, false, true, false]

**Explanation:**
After inserting `1`, `2`, and `3`, `search(0)` is false. After inserting `4`, `search(1)` is true. `erase(0)` is false because `0` is absent. `erase(1)` removes one occurrence, so the final `search(1)` is false.

## Constraints

* `0 <= num, target <= 20000`
* At most `50000` calls are made to `search`, `add`, and `erase`.
* Duplicate values must be erased one occurrence at a time.

examples.output: [null, null, null, null, false, null, true, false, true, false]

solutions.name: Probabilistic Node Tower Skiplist
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n log n) worst-case pointer slots, O(n) expected promoted nodes per level distribution
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store each value in a node that owns an array of forward pointers. To search, start at the highest non-empty level, move right while the next value is smaller than the target, then drop one level. Insert records the predecessor at every level, creates a random-height node, and splices that node into each promoted level. Erase uses the same predecessor path and unlinks one matching node.

## Key Insight

The search path is the reusable work. Once the predecessor before `num` is known at every level, insertion and deletion are just local pointer rewrites.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: Expected O(log n) for search, add, and erase.
- Space Complexity: O(n) nodes plus their promoted forward pointers.

solutions.name: Array Cursor Probabilistic Skiplist
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(C * L) array slots for inserted nodes and levels
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use integer node ids instead of object references. Slot `0` is the head sentinel. `value[id]` stores the key and `next[id][level]` stores the next node id, with `0` meaning null. Search, insertion, and deletion are the same predecessor-path algorithm as an object skiplist.

## Key Insight

A skiplist is a set of links. Those links can be represented as array indices, which is useful when teaching pointer structure separately from object allocation.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: Expected O(log n) for each operation.
- Space Complexity: O(number of inserted nodes * max levels).

solutions.name: Deterministic Promotion Skiplist
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) typical when insertion count distributes tower heights
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same node-tower and predecessor-path structure as the probabilistic skiplist, but choose the height from the insertion counter: every second insert gets level 2, every fourth insert gets level 3, and so on. The implementation is deterministic while preserving the layered-list idea.

## Key Insight

Randomness is not the only way to teach promotion. The essential invariant is that higher levels are sparser ordered lists that accelerate the level-0 scan.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n) typical for well-distributed insertion counts; O(n) worst case remains possible.
- Space Complexity: O(n) nodes and promoted links.

solutions.name: Sorted Dynamic Array Multiset
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) search plus O(n) insertion/deletion shifts
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep all values in a sorted dynamic array. Binary search finds the first position whose value is at least the target. Search checks that position. Add shifts the suffix right and inserts at the lower bound. Erase removes one occurrence by shifting the suffix left.

## Key Insight

This is a deliberate contrast route. It shows that sorted order alone gives fast search, but without links or towers, insertion and deletion pay for moving contiguous storage.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n) to locate a value, O(n) to insert or erase because elements shift.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Counting Array Multiset Baseline
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(U), where U is the value range
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the constraint `0 <= num, target <= 20000`. Store the occurrence count for each possible value. Search tests whether the count is positive; add increments the count; erase decrements exactly one copy when present.

## Key Insight

This is not a general skiplist, but it is an important constraint-driven baseline: when the key universe is tiny, direct addressing can beat a sophisticated probabilistic structure while still handling duplicates correctly.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) for search, add, and erase.
- Space Complexity: O(U) for the fixed value universe.

tests.description: Duplicate values require erase to remove one copy at a time.
Boundary values at both ends of the allowed key range.
Erasing a missing value between present values must not damage neighbors.
Three duplicate copies disappear over three successful erase calls.
Descending insert order still keeps searches and erases correct.
After a value is fully removed, the structure can add it again and erase it again.
Deleting one middle value must preserve predecessor and successor search paths.
Mixed insertions and deletions catch stale pointer or stale count mistakes.
